title: Intelligent Practice
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton explains Intelligent Practice, a sequence of questions in which each differs from the last by one carefully chosen change, and offers ten tips for using it. The rationale is variation theory: when one element varies and the rest is held constant, students are pushed to notice the element that moved. He frames the student routine as Reflect, Expect, Check, Explain, and argues the real value comes when an expectation fails and forces deeper thinking. The tips cover when to start (after plain fluency practice), how to prompt each stage, and when to run it as a whole-class sequence one reveal at a time. He also warns against over-writing and suggests spin-offs such as Fill in the Gaps and Variation Spiders. It is a practical guide for a maths teacher wanting practice that builds understanding rather than autopilot.
points: Intelligent Practice changes one thing between consecutive questions so students must attend to the relationship, not just run the procedure.
Reflect, Expect, Check, Explain gives students skin in the game, since having predicted an answer they want to find out if they were right.
Fluency should come first: students short on procedural confidence cannot also attend to the relationships between examples.
Running a sequence with the whole class, revealing one example at a time, lets the teacher steer the thinking but risks pace mismatches, so switch to independent work after the first few.
Asking for a written explanation of just one relationship, rather than writing at every stage, keeps the thinking from being swamped by the paperwork.
quotes: Intelligent Practice is a type of practice where consecutive questions are carefully related to each other. Usually, just one thing has changed between one question and the next.

By holding constant as much as possible and varying one element, we can direct students’ attention to that element that has varied. Any change (or lack of) in the answer or approach to getting the answer may then be attributed to the change in the element.

I call this process Reflect, Expect, Check, Explain. This can lead to significant moments of revelation and discussion when these expectations are not realised, compelling students to think more deeply about the processes involved, instead of just cruising through a sequence of questions on autopilot.

If students do not have a certain competence and confidence with the procedure, they will be unable to attend sufficiently to the relationships and thus not get much out of Intelligent Practice. A few warm-up questions on the topic where students do not need to think about the relationship between them will help.

One of the benefits of the Expect phase is it makes these examples mean more to students. Having formed an expectation, students are now very keen to find out if they are correct or not - they have skin in the game.

The advantages of this approach are that you can direct all students to Reflect, Expect, Check and Explain, and coordinate a discussion where students hear the thinking of several of their classmates. The disadvantage is that not everyone works at the same speed, so you are likely to move too quickly for some, and too slowly for others.

In the early days, I used to ask students to write me a sentence for Reflect, a sentence for Expect, show all their working for Check, and then potentially a paragraph for Explain. This was too much for some students, took too long, and got in the way of their mathematical thinking.
